steps.title: Recruit at least three board directors
steps.detail: Alaska nonprofits need a board, and secondary sources put the minimum at three directors with a president, secretary and treasurer (confirm in AS 10.20). Pick people who are not related to each other or to Jeremy by family or business. The IRS and funders look hard at boards made up of relatives or business partners. A veteran, someone with finance skills and a clinician or outdoor professional would be a strong first three.

steps.title: Confirm the name is free to use
steps.detail: Search the Alaska corporations database for 'Last Frontier Corps' and close variants, and search the federal trademark database. Similar names already used by other Alaska organizations can get the filing rejected or cause confusion with donors. Also confirm who owns the lastfrontiercorps.org domain.

steps.title: Call the Foraker Group
steps.detail: Foraker is Alaska's nonprofit support organization, based in Anchorage (907-743-1200). They advise startups and can tell you whether a fiscal sponsor makes sense. One conversation here can save months.

steps.title: Decide whether to start under a fiscal sponsor
steps.detail: A fiscal sponsor is an existing 501(c)(3) that accepts donations and grants on your behalf while your own status is pending. Foraker runs one called Sultana, with an administrative fee reported at about 9 to 15 percent. It lets you take tax-deductible gifts and run a pilot trip sooner. The trade-off is the fee and less control. You can also skip this and wait for your own IRS letter.

steps.title: Separate the nonprofit from Jeremy's guiding business
steps.detail: Jeremy guides for a living, and the nonprofit will need guiding. If the nonprofit ever pays Jeremy or his business, that is a related-party transaction. It is allowed, but only with a written conflict-of-interest policy, a board vote he sits out, and rates no higher than market. Decide now whether he will be paid staff, donate his time, or be hired as a contractor, and write it down.

steps.title: Write the Articles of Incorporation with IRS language
steps.detail: Alaska's nonprofit articles form is short. The IRS also requires specific wording: a purpose clause limiting the organization to 501(c)(3) charitable purposes, and a dissolution clause sending leftover assets to another charity. Add both as an attachment, or the IRS application will fail later. Describe the activity as wilderness trips that support veteran mental health. Do not describe it as guided fishing or hunting, which reads like a recreation business.

steps.title: Name a registered agent with an Alaska address
steps.detail: The state needs a person or company with a physical Alaska street address who can receive legal mail. Jeremy can be the agent if he has a stable Alaska address.

steps.title: File the articles with the State of Alaska
steps.detail: File online with the Division of Corporations, Business and Professional Licensing. The current official form lists a $50 nonrefundable fee.

steps.title: Get an EIN from the IRS
steps.detail: The Employer Identification Number is the organization's tax ID. Apply online after the state approves the articles. It is free and issued immediately. Never pay a third-party site for this.
steps.when: Same day the articles are approved

steps.title: Adopt bylaws
steps.detail: The rules for how the board runs: number of directors, terms, officers, meetings, voting. Foraker and many law firms publish Alaska templates.

steps.title: Adopt a conflict-of-interest policy
steps.detail: The IRS publishes a sample policy in the Form 1023 instructions. This matters more than usual here because of Jeremy's guiding business.

steps.title: Hold the first board meeting and keep minutes
steps.detail: Adopt the bylaws and conflict policy, elect officers, authorize a bank account and approve applying for 501(c)(3) status. Written minutes are the proof.
steps.when: Right after the articles are approved

steps.title: Get an Alaska business license
steps.detail: A state form says a business license is required for a new entity doing business in Alaska. The fee is reported as about $50 a year. Ask the Division whether your nonprofit needs one, since I could not confirm the nonprofit rule on an official page.

steps.title: Open a bank account in the organization's name
steps.detail: Needs the EIN, approved articles and the board resolution. Never run nonprofit money through a personal account.

steps.title: File the initial report with the state
steps.detail: Due within six months of incorporation. It lists the officers and directors.

steps.title: Check which IRS form you qualify for
steps.detail: Form 1023-EZ is the short version. You qualify only if you expect gross receipts of $50,000 or less in each of the next three years and hold assets of $250,000 or less. Work through the eligibility worksheet in the instructions. If you expect a large grant early, use the full Form 1023.

steps.title: File the IRS application on Pay.gov
steps.detail: The 1023-EZ fee is reported as $275 and the full Form 1023 as $600. The EZ is far quicker to prepare and usually decided sooner. The fee is not refunded if you file the EZ and turn out not to qualify. File within 27 months of incorporating so the exemption reaches back to the day the corporation was formed.
steps.when: Within 27 months of incorporating, sooner is better

steps.title: Receive and file the IRS determination letter
steps.detail: This letter is the proof of 501(c)(3) status. Every grant maker and donation platform asks for it. Keep a PDF where the whole board can reach it.

steps.title: Put the annual IRS filing on the calendar
steps.detail: Small nonprofits file Form 990-N, a short online postcard, every year. Missing it three years in a row cancels the tax exemption automatically.

steps.title: Register as a charity with the Alaska Department of Law
steps.detail: Alaska requires charities to register before asking the public for money, and to renew by September 1 each year. The fee is reported as $40. An organization that will not raise more than $5,000 in a fiscal year (not counting government grants) is exempt and can file a Notice of Exemption instead.
steps.when: Before the first public ask, then every September 1

steps.title: Check fundraising rules for other states
steps.detail: A donate button reaches people everywhere, and many states require registration before you solicit their residents. This is low priority while giving is small and local. Ask Foraker when it starts to matter.

steps.title: Buy insurance
steps.detail: Taking veterans into remote country carries real risk. Get quotes for general liability that explicitly covers guided wilderness activities, directors and officers coverage for the board, and participant accident coverage. Land permits usually require proof of liability insurance.

steps.title: Write participant paperwork and safety plans
steps.detail: A liability waiver, medical and emergency contact form, a backcountry emergency and evacuation plan, and a written protocol for a mental health crisis on a trip. Have an Alaska attorney review the waiver.

steps.title: Get land-use permits for where trips will run
steps.detail: Guided trips on public land usually need a permit from whoever manages the land: a Commercial Use Authorization in national parks, a special use authorization in national forests, a commercial use permit in Alaska state parks. Being a nonprofit does not exempt you by itself. Ask each agency how they treat a trip that is free to participants.

steps.title: Confirm licences for trips that include fishing or hunting
steps.detail: The trips are general wilderness trips, so most need no fishing or hunting guide licence. On a trip where veterans do fish or hunt, guiding rules can apply: Alaska regulates guided sport fishing and, more strictly, guided big game hunting. Ask the Alaska Department of Fish and Game and the state guide licensing board what covers a nonprofit trip where this is incidental. Keep wilderness first aid certifications current for every trip.

steps.title: Board adopts the fishing and hunting policy
steps.detail: A draft policy is in the website repository at governance/fishing-and-hunting-policy.md. It says trips are wilderness trips and not guided fishing or hunting, participants hold their own licences, and nobody is compensated for assisting. It takes effect only when the board votes to adopt it and records that in the minutes. Do the agency confirmation in the step above first, and have an Alaska attorney look it over if you can.

steps.title: Line up a licensed mental health advisor
steps.detail: The website says the program complements professional treatment. Back that up with a licensed clinician who advises on trip design, participant screening and crisis response. Funders in veteran mental health will ask who this is.

steps.title: Put the state biennial report on the calendar
steps.detail: Alaska nonprofits file a report every two years to stay in good standing. Sources disagree on the fee, so check the Division's site.

steps.title: Set up online donations
steps.detail: Pick a donation platform, connect it to the organization's bank account and replace the Give button on the website, which currently leads to the contact form. Most platforms need the EIN and the IRS letter, or a fiscal sponsor.

steps.title: Send donor receipts
steps.detail: The IRS requires a written acknowledgment for any single gift of $250 or more, stating the amount and that nothing was given in return. Most donation platforms send these automatically.

steps.title: Set up bookkeeping and a first-year budget
steps.detail: Track every dollar in and out from day one. Write a simple budget that shows the cost of one trip and the cost per veteran. Grant applications ask for both.

steps.title: Run a pilot trip and document it
steps.detail: Nearly every funder wants evidence the program works. One small trip with a few veterans, photos taken with permission, short before-and-after feedback forms and a few quotes will do more for fundraising than any document.
steps.when: As soon as phase 4 is done

steps.title: Write a one-page case for support
steps.detail: Who you serve, what a trip is, what it costs, what changes for the veteran, and who is behind it. Jeremy's own story is the core. This becomes the base of every grant application.

steps.title: Claim a Candid profile
steps.detail: Candid (formerly GuideStar) is where funders look nonprofits up. Claim the profile and fill it in to earn a transparency seal.

steps.title: Register in SAM.gov
steps.detail: Required for any federal grant, including the VA programs. It is free and issues the organization's Unique Entity ID. Approval can take weeks, so start well before a grant deadline. Never pay a third party to register.
steps.when: After the EIN and bank account

steps.title: Update the website with real details
steps.detail: Add the real EIN, confirmed programs, a working application form and Jeremy's photo. The placeholder list is in the repository README.

steps.title: Individual donors and local businesses
steps.detail: First money for almost every new nonprofit. Start with people who know Jeremy, then Alaska outfitters, lodges, veteran-owned businesses, and VFW and American Legion posts. Gear and lodging donated in kind count too.
steps.when: Start once you can legally accept gifts

steps.title: Rasmuson Foundation Tier 1 grant
steps.detail: Alaska's largest private funder. Tier 1 grants are reported at up to $35,000, with applications accepted year-round and decisions in about 90 days. First-time applicants are steered to Tier 1. Confirm on the foundation's site whether IRS status is required and what the current cap is.

steps.title: Alaska Mental Health Trust Authority
steps.detail: Funds organizations serving Trust beneficiaries, which include Alaskans with mental illness, substance use disorders and traumatic brain injury. Veterans with those conditions fall inside that group. Check current criteria for partnership grants on the Trust's site.

steps.title: Alaska Community Foundation
steps.detail: Runs grant programs and local affiliate funds across the state. I have not researched its current programs in detail. Worth a look once the IRS letter is in hand.

steps.title: VA Staff Sergeant Fox Suicide Prevention Grant
steps.detail: Federal grants of $100,000 to $750,000 a year to community groups doing veteran suicide prevention, with no match required. The 2026 window closed June 12 and no next date is announced. Applications are heavy and reviewers expect a track record, so treat this as a year-two goal. Needs SAM.gov registration.

steps.title: VA Adaptive Sports Grant
steps.detail: Federal grants for adaptive sports programs for disabled veterans, up to $750,000 per organization. The 2026 round closed in May and the next depends on Congress renewing the program. This is a weak fit as things stand: the trips are general wilderness trips, not a sports program, and it only fits if they are built for veterans with disabilities.

steps.title: Bob Woodruff Foundation
steps.detail: National funder of veteran programs. Listings say applicants need financial statements and two years of gross receipts above $50,000, which makes this a year-three target. Confirm on their site.

steps.title: Pick.Click.Give
steps.detail: Lets Alaskans donate part of their Permanent Fund Dividend to listed nonprofits. I have not checked the entry rules, so look them up once the organization has its IRS letter.
